records.sourceFile: Scheduling concurrent training 48 vs 72 hours after simulated match play - Effects on neuromuscular function and fatigue.pdf

paper.citation: Cross R, Lovell R, Marshall PW, Norris D, Siegler JC. Scheduling Concurrent Training 48 versus 72 h after Simulated Match Play: Effects on Neuromuscular Function and Fatigue. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2023;55(2):301-310.
paper.abstract: Ten male recreational team sport athletes completed two 5-day microcycles that began with a simulated soccer match, with concurrent training scheduled 48 h (MD+2) or 72 h (MD+3) later. Neuromuscular function recovered within 24 h in both conditions. Fatigue was higher at 48 and 72 h in MD+2, while fatigue remained above baseline at 96 h after concurrent training on MD+3.
paper.tldr: Scheduling concurrent training 48 h after a simulated match did not slow neuromuscular recovery compared with 72 h. Training at 72 h left athletes more fatigued at 96 h, the day before the next match in a 5-day microcycle.
paper.methods: Within-subject comparison in 10 male recreational team sport athletes across two counterbalanced 5-day microcycles, with concurrent training (an intermittent sprint protocol followed 1 h later by a lower limb resistance session) on MD+2 or MD+3. Maximal voluntary force, potentiated twitch, voluntary activation, EMG, POMS fatigue and quadriceps soreness were measured at baseline, after the simulated match, every 24 h to 96 h, and around the training session. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used.
paper.findings: Immediately after the simulated match, maximal voluntary force fell 14.6% and potentiated twitch force fell 31.5%, recovering by 48 h and 24 h respectively. Neuromuscular function was back at baseline before both training sessions; immediately after concurrent training, force and twitch fell again (about 21% and 47%), with no difference between conditions, and returned to baseline by 24 h. Fatigue was higher in MD+2 than MD+3 at 48 h (5.6 vs 3.3 AU) and 72 h (7.5 vs 2.0 AU), and higher in MD+3 at 96 h (7.9 vs 4.7 AU).
paper.limitations: The sample was small (n=10), the match was a non-contact simulation, and there was no control condition. Voluntary activation and twitch were estimated with 10-Hz doublets, which the authors note may not summate fully. The authors also note that effects below ES 0.71 may have gone undetected.
paper.practicalImplications: In a short in-season microcycle, a concurrent training session 48 h after a match did not impair neuromuscular recovery in these recreational athletes. Athletes felt more fatigued on the day of that session, so their fatigue and soreness reports should be checked when it is scheduled.
paper.athleteDev: For a 5-day in-season microcycle, this study suggests that concurrent training on MD+2 did not compromise neuromuscular recovery compared with MD+3, while MD+3 left athletes more fatigued at 96 h. Early scheduling may keep the late-week plan free for skill and tactical work, but athletes reported higher fatigue at 48 to 72 h.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included healthy recreational athletes only, no injured players, and no contact actions.

records.sourceFile: Small Performance Effects of a Practical Mixed-Methods Cooling Strategy in Elite Team Sport Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Fenemor SP, Gill ND, Driller MW, Mills B, Sella F, Beaven CM. Small Performance Effects of a Practical Mixed-Methods Cooling Strategy in Elite Team Sport Athletes. Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport. 2022.
paper.abstract: Purpose: Ice slurry ingestion and ice towel application can help when used alone, but their combined use had not been tested with a sport-specific test in an elite team sport. Methods: Ten non-heat-acclimated elite male rugby sevens players completed two cycling heat response tests at 35°C and 80% humidity in a crossover design, with (COOLING) and without (HOT) combined internal (ice slushy) and external (ice towels to head, neck and face) pre- and per-cooling. Results: COOLING lowered mean tympanic temperature by 0.4 ± 0.2°C, with non-significant reductions in heart rate, thermal discomfort and thirst, and a non-significant small increase in 4-minute time-trial power. Discussion: Combined cooling gave small physiological, perceptual and performance benefits compared with no cooling.
paper.tldr: An ice slushy plus ice towels on the head, neck and face lowered body temperature in a rugby sevens style heat test, but the performance gain was small and not statistically significant. It is a reasonable cooling option for hot breaks, and fluid intake should be watched because thirst was lower.
paper.methods: Crossover design: ten players completed two heat response tests, each with a 19-minute warm-up, repeated 30-second cycling efforts with six down-ups every second interval, and a 4-minute time trial in a 35°C, 80% humidity chamber. The HOT trial used room-temperature drink; the COOLING trial used 1°C ice slushy at set points and 60 seconds of ice towels. Tympanic temperature, heart rate, perceptual ratings and time-trial power were measured, with testing in consecutive weeks and HOT first.
paper.findings: Mean tympanic temperature was 0.4 ± 0.3°C lower with COOLING (d = 1.18), and this was significant at several time points. Mean heart rate (-5 ± 8 bpm), thermal discomfort (-0.5 ± 0.9 AU) and thirst (-1.0 ± 1.1 AU) were lower, and 4-minute time-trial power was 7 ± 33 W (about 3%) higher, with COOLING, but none of these reached statistical significance. The condition by time interaction was not significant for any variable.
paper.limitations: Ten athletes from one team, no control group, a fixed trial order that confounds condition with week, and tympanic rather than core temperature. The authors also note the cycling protocol reproduces the perceived but not the physiological stress of running, and that athletes were not heat acclimated. The abstract prints the temperature difference as 0.4 ± 0.2°C, while Table 1 gives 0.4 ± 0.3°C (a 95% confidence limit); the table value is used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Combined ice slushy and head, neck and face ice towels lowered tympanic temperature in this test, so the approach is worth trying in hot match conditions, but the study does not show a significant performance gain. Thirst was lower with the slushy, so staff should watch total fluid intake to avoid dehydration.
paper.athleteDev: The 3% time-trial increase was not statistically significant, so performance staff should treat the cooling plan as a heat-management option rather than a proven performance aid. The authors note that heat acclimatisation may give larger benefits, which this study did not test.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. The study tested healthy elite athletes in a heat chamber, with no injured players and no return-to-play outcome.

records.sourceFile: Specific Adaptations to 0 percent, 15 percent, 25 percent, and 50 percent_ Velocity-Loss Thresholds During Bench Press Training.pdf

paper.citation: Rodiles-Guerrero L, Cornejo-Daza PJ, Sánchez-Valdepeñas J, Alcazar J, Rodriguez-López C, Sánchez-Moreno M, et al. Specific Adaptations to 0%, 15%, 25%, and 50% Velocity-Loss Thresholds During Bench Press Training. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022.
paper.abstract: Purpose: To compare four velocity-loss (VL) thresholds (0%, 15%, 25% and 50%) on strength, neuromuscular adaptations and muscle hypertrophy during bench press at 55% to 70% of 1RM. Methods: Fifty resistance-trained men were assigned to four groups for an 8-week, 16-session program that differed in the VL allowed per set. Results: A group by time interaction for 1RM (P = .01) showed gains in all groups except VL0, with the largest gains in VL25; only VL25 increased pectoralis EMG, and only VL50 increased pectoralis cross-sectional area. Conclusions: A VL threshold of about 25% optimised strength and neuromuscular adaptations, while higher thresholds promoted hypertrophy.
paper.tldr: Eight weeks of bench press at 55% to 70% of 1RM with a 25% velocity-loss cutoff gave the largest average 1RM gains, and only the 50% cutoff produced a significant within-group increase in chest muscle size, although the groups did not differ significantly in muscle growth. Choose the cutoff to match the goal, and remember the sample was sport science students, not athletes.
paper.methods: Four groups of resistance-trained men trained bench press twice weekly for 8 weeks, with three sets per session at a set load (55% to 70% of 1RM) and a velocity-loss cutoff of 0%, 15%, 25% or 50% per set. Outcomes were pectoralis cross-sectional area by ultrasound, isometric force and EMG, a progressive loading test with 1RM, and a fatigue test, measured 72 hours before and after training.
paper.findings: 1RM rose in the 15%, 25% and 50% groups (P < .001) but not the 0% group (group by time P = .01), with the largest rise in the 25% group (68.0 to 78.8 kg). Pectoralis cross-sectional area rose only in the 50% group (P < .001), with no group by time interaction. Pectoralis EMG rose only in the 25% group (group by time P = .03), and triceps EMG fell only in the 50% group (P = .006). Isometric force rose in all groups, and most between-group differences in gains were not significant.
paper.limitations: Participants were resistance-trained men, not athletes, and the study covered one exercise, 8 weeks, and one ultrasound slice for muscle size. Randomisation is unclear, as the abstract says random assignment but the Methods describe ABBA counterbalancing by 1RM.
paper.practicalImplications: For bench press at 55% to 70% of 1RM, a 25% velocity-loss cutoff per set looks best for strength and pectoral activation, while a 50% cutoff was the only setting with a significant within-group gain in chest size, alongside lower triceps activity. The authors advise against going beyond a moderate loss, because extra repetitions may not help strength.
paper.athleteDev: The results come from resistance-trained non-athletes, so they should inform strength planning for athletes with caution. The study used a linear velocity transducer, so velocity-loss cutoffs need monitoring equipment, and it does not test athletes or other lifts.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The sample was healthy resistance-trained men, and no injury or rehabilitation outcome was measured.
